job.title: Gradient Descent: Walking Down x Squared

plan.goal: The learner will understand how gradient descent repeatedly steps against the slope to reach a minimum, by following three steps on f(x) = x squared.

scenes.learningPoint: Gradient descent finds the lowest point of a curve by repeatedly stepping downhill.
scenes.visualIntent: Axes with the curve f(x) = x squared sampled from x = -3.5 to 3.5 at 15 points. A dot at x = 3, height 9. A circle marks the bottom at x = 0, labelled 'minimum'.
scenes.narrationSummary: Gradient descent finds the lowest point of a curve. Picture standing on this hill at x equals three, and walking downhill step by step.

scenes.learningPoint: Each step moves x against the slope, scaled by a learning rate.
scenes.visualIntent: Write the rule as text: new x = x − rate × slope. Below: slope of x squared = 2x. A short tangent line at x = 3 labelled 'slope 6', and 'rate = 0.25' written beside it.
scenes.narrationSummary: The slope tells which way is uphill. For x squared the slope is two x, so six at x equals three. We step the other way, scaled by a learning rate, here a quarter.

scenes.learningPoint: Repeating the rule moves x closer to the minimum each time.
scenes.visualIntent: Three arrows on the curve hopping from x = 3 to 1.5 to 0.75 to 0.375. Side table written as text: 3 − 0.25×6 = 1.5; 1.5 − 0.25×3 = 0.75; 0.75 − 0.25×1.5 = 0.375. Heights labelled 9, 2.25, 0.5625, 0.140625.
scenes.narrationSummary: Step one: three minus a quarter of six gives one and a half. Step two: zero point seven five. Step three: zero point three seven five. Each step halves x, and the height drops toward zero.

scenes.learningPoint: The learning rate controls step size: too small is slow, too big overshoots.
scenes.visualIntent: Two small sketches of the curve side by side. Left, 'rate 0.1': short arrow from 3 to 2.4. Right, 'rate 1': arrow jumping from 3 to −3 and back, labelled 'bounces forever'.
scenes.narrationSummary: Step size matters. With rate zero point one, x only moves from three to two point four. With rate one, it jumps to minus three and bounces forever.

limitations: Uses one simple curve with a single lowest point; real problems have many variables and can have several valleys.
The learning rate values are illustrative, chosen so the arithmetic stays clean.
